title: What are the rules for `this()` and `super()` calls in constructors — each must be the FIRST statement so you can use at most one per constructor, `super()` is implicitly inserted if you write neither, and constructor chaining via `this(...)` delegates to another constructor in the same class — and what happens if the superclass has no no-arg constructor (compile error unless you explicitly call `super(args)`)?
shortTitle: What are the rules for this() and super() in constructors, and what happens if the superclass has no no-arg constructor?

s1_definition.profdef: Within a constructor, `this(...)` delegates to another constructor of the SAME class and `super(...)` invokes a constructor of the DIRECT superclass. Either call, if present, must be the very first statement of the constructor, which means a constructor can contain at most one of them. If you write neither, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument `super()` as the first statement. Constructor chaining with `this(...)` lets several overloaded constructors funnel into one primary constructor so initialization logic is not duplicated. If the superclass has no accessible no-argument constructor, the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied, so you must explicitly call an available `super(args)` as the first statement, otherwise the code does not compile.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of building an account record as a signing ceremony with a strict order. Before Rajesh's specific account details are stamped, the base bank-customer record must be established first, so super runs before the subclass body. The rule that this or super must be the first line is like the bank insisting the foundation is laid before any walls, and you only lay one foundation, so at most one of them per constructor. If you do not explicitly lay a foundation, the bank automatically lays the default one, the implicit no-arg super. But if the base record type offers no default foundation and only a detailed one requiring information, you are forced to explicitly provide that information with super and arguments, or the whole building plan is rejected, which is the compile error.
s1_definition.oneliner: this() delegates within the class and super() to the parent, at most one and it must be first, super() is auto-inserted if you write neither, and a parent with no no-arg constructor forces you to call super with arguments.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Within a constructor, `this(...)` delegates to another constructor of the SAME class and `super(...)` invokes a constructor of the DIRECT superclass. Either call, if present, must be the very first statement of the constructor, which means a constructor can contain at most one of them. If you write neither, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument `super()` as the first statement. Constructor chaining with `this(...)` lets several overloaded constructors funnel into one primary constructor so initialization logic is not duplicated. If the superclass has no accessible no-argument constructor, the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied, so you must explicitly call an available `super(args)` as the first statement, otherwise the code does not compile.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of building an account record as a signing ceremony with a strict order. Before Rajesh's specific account details are stamped, the base bank-customer record must be established first, so super runs before the subclass body. The rule that this or super must be the first line is like the bank insisting the foundation is laid before any walls, and you only lay one foundation, so at most one of them per constructor. If you do not explicitly lay a foundation, the bank automatically lays the default one, the implicit no-arg super. But if the base record type offers no default foundation and only a detailed one requiring information, you are forced to explicitly provide that information with super and arguments, or the whole building plan is rejected, which is the compile error.

**One line to remember:** this() delegates within the class and super() to the parent, at most one and it must be first, super() is auto-inserted if you write neither, and a parent with no no-arg constructor forces you to call super with arguments.

sections.s2_technical:
`this(args)` calls another constructor in the same class, which is how you chain overloaded constructors so they share one real initialization path. For example a class with a two-argument and a three-argument constructor can have the two-argument one call `this(a, b, DEFAULT_C)` so all the validation and assignment lives in the three-argument constructor only. This avoids duplicating logic and keeps a single source of truth for how an object is built.

`super(args)` calls a constructor of the direct superclass, and it exists because an object must be fully initialized from the top of the hierarchy downward. The superclass part of the object must be constructed before the subclass adds its own fields, so super runs first and establishes the inherited state. For example a SavingsAccount constructor calls `super(accountId, holderName)` to initialize the base Account fields before setting its own interest rate.

The first-statement rule is strict: whichever of this or super you use must be the first statement in the constructor body, and because both occupy that same single slot, you can use at most one of them per constructor. You cannot call both, and you cannot put any executable statement before them. The reason is that the language guarantees the superclass is initialized before any subclass code runs, which would be impossible if arbitrary statements ran first. A modern nuance is that recent Java versions relax this slightly to allow some statements that do not reference the instance before an explicit this or super, but the classic and safest mental model is first-statement-only.

Implicit super insertion is a key rule. If a constructor contains neither a this nor a super call, the compiler automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor, `super()`, as the first statement. This is why a class with no explicit constructor still correctly initializes its parent: the default constructor the compiler generates contains an implicit `super()`. So every constructor eventually chains up to the ultimate superclass Object's constructor.

The compile-error case follows directly. The implicit `super()` requires the superclass to HAVE an accessible no-argument constructor. If the superclass declares only constructors that take arguments, then there is no no-argument constructor, because declaring any constructor suppresses the compiler's default one. In that situation the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied, and the subclass constructor must explicitly call an available `super(args)` as its first statement, or the code fails to compile with a message that there is no default constructor in the superclass. A senior engineer stresses designing base classes thoughtfully: if a base class requires arguments, every subclass is forced to pass them up, which is often desirable for mandatory invariants, and that constructor chaining via this is the clean way to provide convenient overloads while keeping all validation in one canonical constructor. They also note that final fields must be assigned exactly once along every constructor path, which chaining helps guarantee, and that heavy logic in constructors is a smell, favoring factory methods or builders for complex construction.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India models accounts with a base Account class and a SavingsAccount subclass, and constructor rules shaped the design and caused a real compile issue.

Problem 1 — the account classes had several convenient constructors, such as one that defaulted the opening balance to zero, and duplicating the validation across them caused a bug where one constructor skipped a check. The fix funnels every overload through one primary constructor using this chaining, so validation lives in exactly one place. This is exactly constructor chaining with this.

Problem 2 — the base Account class required an account id and a holder name, so it had no no-argument constructor, and when a new subclass was written without an explicit super call, it failed to compile because the implicit no-arg super could not be satisfied. Adding an explicit super with arguments fixed it. This is exactly the no-no-arg-constructor compile error.

Problem 3 — the team needed the base Account part to be fully initialized before the SavingsAccount set its interest rate, which is naturally guaranteed because super runs first.

The fix defines a base Account with only an arguments constructor, a SavingsAccount that calls super with arguments and chains its own convenience constructor with this, and demonstrates the implicit super and the first-statement rule. The code defines an `Account` base class, a `SavingsAccount` subclass, and a demo that builds Rajesh's savings account two ways. The demo shows the chaining order through log output.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's savings account built with all four arguments including an explicit rate, and Priya's savings account built with three arguments letting the rate default.

Step 1. Building Rajesh invokes the primary four-argument SavingsAccount constructor. Its very first statement is an explicit super call with the account id, holder name, and balance, which is mandatory because the base Account class has no no-argument constructor. The super call runs first and initializes the inherited Account fields.

Step 2. After super returns, the SavingsAccount body runs, validating and assigning the interest rate of zero point zero six five zero. Because super completed first, the inherited state is fully set before the subclass touches its own field, which is the guaranteed top-down initialization order.

Step 3. Building Priya invokes the three-argument convenience constructor. Its first and only statement is a this call that delegates to the primary four-argument constructor, passing the default rate constant. Because this occupies the first-statement slot, the convenience constructor cannot also call super, and it does not need to, since the primary constructor it delegates to will.

Step 4. The delegated primary constructor then runs exactly as in step one: explicit super first to initialize the base Account fields for Priya, then the body to validate and assign the default rate of zero point zero four zero zero. All validation lives in that single primary constructor, so there is no duplication and no risk of one overload skipping a check.

Step 5. Both accounts are now fully constructed, and the describe method reports each one's id, holder, balance, and rate. The fine-level logs, if shown, reveal the order: the Account super initialization logs before the SavingsAccount body logs for each construction, confirming super-before-body.

Step 6. The demo logs Rajesh with his explicit rate and Priya with the defaulted rate, demonstrating this chaining for convenience overloads, mandatory explicit super because the base lacks a no-arg constructor, and the top-down initialization order.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 19:31:30 [INFO] Rajesh: SAV2001 / Rajesh Kumar / balance=1000000.00 / rate=0.0650
2026-10-30 19:31:30 [INFO] Priya: CUR3001 / Priya Sharma / balance=250000.00 / rate=0.0400
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Full constructor (Rajesh) ──
  new SavingsAccount(id, name, bal, 0.0650)
    │ super(id, name, bal)   ← FIRST statement (mandatory: no no-arg parent ctor)
    │     Account fields initialized (top-down)
    ▼
    SavingsAccount body: validate + set interestRate=0.0650

  ── Convenience constructor (Priya) ──
  new SavingsAccount(id, name, bal)
    │ this(id, name, bal, DEFAULT_RATE)   ← FIRST statement (delegate in-class)
    ▼
    → PRIMARY SavingsAccount(id, name, bal, 0.0400)
        │ super(id, name, bal)   ← runs first
        ▼ body: set interestRate=0.0400

  ── Rules ──
  at most ONE of this()/super() per ctor, and it MUST be first.
  write neither → compiler inserts super() (no-arg).
  parent has NO no-arg ctor → must call super(args) explicitly or COMPILE ERROR.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Constructor Chaining Rules ═══

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  One PRIMARY constructor holds all validation; overloads chain  │
  │     via this(...) (DRY, single source of truth).                │
  │  Base requires args → subclass MUST super(args) (enforces        │
  │     mandatory invariants at construction).                      │
  │  super runs before subclass body → top-down initialization.     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Rules (as prose) ───────────────────────────────────────────
  this(args): delegate to another ctor of the SAME class.
  super(args): invoke DIRECT superclass ctor. Each must be the FIRST
  statement → at most one per ctor. Write neither → implicit super().
  Parent with no no-arg ctor → explicit super(args) required or compile error.

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │            Account           │  (base — args-only ctor)
  │  - accountId: String         │
  │  - holderName: String        │
  │  - balance: BigDecimal       │
  │  + Account(id, name, balance)│  NO no-arg ctor exists
  └──────────────▲───────────────┘
                 │ extends (super must be called with args)
  ┌──────────────┴───────────────┐
  │        SavingsAccount        │
  │  - interestRate: BigDecimal  │
  │  + SavingsAccount(id,name,   │  PRIMARY: super(...) first + validate
  │      bal, rate)              │
  │  + SavingsAccount(id,name,   │  CONVENIENCE: this(...) → primary
  │      bal)                    │
  │  + describe(): String        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. new SavingsAccount(id,name,bal,rate) → super(id,name,bal) → body
  2. new SavingsAccount(id,name,bal) → this(id,name,bal,DEFAULT) → primary
  3. primary → super(id,name,bal) → set rate

  Contract for SavingsAccount(id,name,bal,rate):
    Pre:  base fields non-null; rate non-null and non-negative
    Post: Account part initialized first (super), then interestRate set
    Note: explicit super(args) is REQUIRED (Account has no no-arg ctor)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Within a constructor, this with arguments delegates to another constructor of the same class, and super with arguments invokes a constructor of the direct superclass. Whichever of these you use must be the very first statement of the constructor, and because they both occupy that single first slot, a constructor can contain at most one of them, never both, and nothing executable may precede them. The reason is that the language guarantees the superclass part of the object is fully initialized before any subclass code runs, which top-down ordering would be impossible to promise if arbitrary statements ran first.

If a constructor contains neither a this nor a super call, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument super as the first statement. That is why a class with no explicit constructor still correctly initializes its parent, because the default constructor the compiler generates contains that implicit super, and every constructor ultimately chains up to Object's constructor. Constructor chaining with this is how I provide convenient overloads while keeping all the real initialization and validation in one primary constructor, so there is a single source of truth and no duplicated checks.

The compile-error case follows from the implicit super rule. The implicit no-argument super requires the superclass to have an accessible no-argument constructor. But declaring any constructor suppresses the compiler's default one, so a base class that declares only constructors with arguments has no no-argument constructor. In that case the implicit super cannot be satisfied, and the subclass constructor must explicitly call an available super with arguments as its first statement, or the code fails to compile. That is often desirable, because it forces every subclass to supply the mandatory information the base class needs.

In our account model at National Bank of India, the base Account class requires an account id, a holder name, and a balance, so it has no no-argument constructor. When a new SavingsAccount subclass was written without an explicit super call, it failed to compile, and adding an explicit super with arguments fixed it, which is exactly the rule in action. I funnel the SavingsAccount's convenience constructor through its primary four-argument constructor using this delegation, so all the validation lives in one place and a bug we once had, where one overload skipped a check, cannot recur. And because super always runs before the subclass body, the inherited Account fields are guaranteed to be set before SavingsAccount assigns its interest rate, giving clean top-down initialization.
